newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Time to send in the Internet Mounties?.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Time to send in the Internet Mounties?.

text.p: You could call it the World Wild Web because on the Internet just about anything goes.
That is just the way many people like it. It is an arena mostly -- although not completely -- beyond the long arm of the government and the regulatory-minded.
Yet not everyone is happy with that and some keen minds are at work on ways of sending in the Cyber Mounties or marshals to bring a little law and order to the new digital frontier.

Legal beagles are becoming fascinated with the growing personal and commercial life on the Internet and the new ideas needed to bring some legal order to a place that defies traditional definitions and prescriptions.

A number of court actions have been taken against sites and content on the Net, but some legal experts have realized the folly of trying to regulate a system that knows no boundaries. They are realizing the Internet will likely become increasingly impervious to the laws of any country.

For example, if a company was libeled on the Internet from someone posting a message from a computer server in the United Kingdom, would the company seek justice in its home country or in the United Kingdom?
Worse still, what if someone wrote the offending statements while in Canada and sent the note sent over the Net to be stored and accessed from the United Kingdom?
That is small potatoes compared to problems that could crop up in the near future. While child pornography is a growing concern on the Net, a number of other issues are waiting to explode.

What happens if local authorities want to ban gambling in a country where citizens have access to gambling houses on the Net? What if a bank chartered in one country accepts customers from another and breaks local financial regulations?
There are no simple answers to those questions because old notions of legal systems defined by national borders have gone the way of 2400-baud modems.

"Global computer-based communications cut across territorial borders, creating a new realm of human activity and undermining the feasibility -- and legitimacy -- of applying laws based on geographic boundaries," wrote David Johnson and David Post in a paper entitled "Law and Borders -- The Rise of Law in Cyberspace."

The paper, which can be found at the Washington-based Cyberspace Law Institute (www.cli.org), basically advocated that Cyberspace be considered a separate entity unrelated to the "real" world made up of atoms.

"Many of the jurisdictional and substantive quandaries raised by border-crossing electronic communications could be resolved by one simple principle: conceiving of Cyberspace as a distinct "place" for purposes of legal analysis by recognizing a legally significant border between Cyberspace and the "real world," the authors stated.

Some have suggested that a Law of the Sea-type convention could be drafted, but that would involve international cooperation. It would also be resisted by many dedicated Web heads who would not welcome a bureaucratic process for an arena blessedly free of all that.

Others have suggested more of a self-regulatory process where a Web kangaroo court could be set up, with the ultimate punishment being banishment. The court could issue Internet certificates with a unique number that could be withdrawn from netizens who violated Web 'netiquette.'
But even that would be resisted by many to whom it smacks of a big brother-type system, complete with an all-controlling personal identification number.
